excerpt: Follow this guide to navigate the claims process and get fair payment for your vehicle damage and injuries.
keyTakeaways: Georgia car accident victims can recover economic damages for medical bills and lost wages, non-economic damages for pain and suffering, and, where clear and convincing evidence shows willful or wanton conduct, punitive damages — capped at $250,000 in most cases, but uncapped when the driver intended harm or was substantially impaired by alcohol or drugs (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1). For claims arising on or after April 21, 2025, medical damages are limited to the reasonable value of necessary care, and the jury may hear both what was billed and what your health insurer paid (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-1.1). For lawsuits commenced on or after April 21, 2025, O.C.G.A. § 40-8-76.1(d) lets the defense use seat-belt non-use as evidence. Georgia is an at-fault state with 25/50/25 minimum insurance requirements. The modified comparative fault rule (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) bars recovery at 50% or more fault, and the two-year statute of limitations (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) sets a strict filing deadline.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a car accident claim in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Georgia's statute of limitations gives you two years from the date of the accident to file a personal injury lawsuit under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. Vehicle and other property damage claims have a separate four-year deadline (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-31). Missing the personal injury deadline typically means permanently losing your right to compensation.

faqs.question: What is Georgia's minimum car insurance requirement?
faqs.answer: Georgia requires all drivers to carry minimum liability insurance of 25/50/25 under O.C.G.A. § 40-9-37 — meaning $25,000 per person, $50,000 per accident for bodily injury, and $25,000 for property damage. These minimums are often insufficient to cover serious injuries.

faqs.question: How does comparative fault work in Georgia car accidents?
faqs.answer: Under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, Georgia follows a modified comparative fault rule. Your compensation is reduced by your percentage of fault. If you are found 50% or more at fault, you cannot recover any damages. Insurance companies aggressively try to assign blame to reduce payouts.

faqs.question: Should I give a recorded statement to the insurance company after a Georgia car accident?
faqs.answer: No. You are not legally required to give a recorded statement to the at-fault driver's insurance company, and doing so often hurts your claim. Adjusters are trained to ask questions designed to elicit admissions that can be used to reduce or deny your compensation. Your own policy may require cooperation with your own insurer, so talk to a lawyer before giving it a statement.

faqs.question: Can I recover punitive damages after a Georgia car accident?
faqs.answer: Yes, if clear and convincing evidence shows the at-fault driver's conduct was willful, wanton, or showed a conscious indifference to consequences — ordinary carelessness is not enough. Under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1, punitive damages are generally capped at $250,000, but there is no cap when the defendant intended to cause harm or was under the influence of alcohol or drugs to the degree that judgment was substantially impaired, or in product liability cases.

faqs.question: What if the at-fault driver in my Georgia accident is uninsured?
faqs.answer: If you carry uninsured motorist (UM) coverage on your own policy, you can file a claim with your own insurer. Georgia auto policies include UM coverage unless you rejected it in writing (O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11), so check your declarations page. Without UM coverage, you may need to pursue a personal lawsuit against the uninsured driver directly.
